name: Papal primacy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 1 (1870)
defined.quote: a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole church of God was immediately and directly promised to the blessed apostle Peter and conferred on him by Christ the lord.

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 2 (1870)
defined.quote: Therefore whoever succeeds to the chair of Peter obtains by the institution of Christ himself, the primacy of Peter over the whole church.
the holy apostolic see and the Roman pontiff holds the primacy over the whole world and the Roman pontiff is the successor of blessed Peter prince of the apostles

proposition: The bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, holds by Christ's institution a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church, not only a primacy of honor.
elements: Christ gave Peter a primacy among the apostles that included authority, not only honor
This primacy passes to Peter's successors in the see of Rome
The Roman bishop's authority extends over the whole Church, not only his own region
Other churches and bishops must agree with, or may be judged by, the Roman see
precursors: Peter as first or leader among the apostles
Rome as a church of special apostolic standing because Peter and Paul taught and died there
Communion with Rome as a mark of sound faith
Appeals or letters sent to the Roman bishop from other regions
Rome having the first place of honor among the great sees
incompatible: All bishops are equal in authority and none may judge another
The Roman bishop's rank comes only from the city's civil importance
The rock of Matthew 16 is Peter's faith or confession only, with no office passed to successors
A council may overrule or depose the Roman bishop as a superior authority
queries: the church of the Romans presides
Peter the rock on which the church is built
appeal to the bishop of Rome
keys of the kingdom given to Peter
bishop of Rome judges other bishops
first_defined: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439); defined in full at the First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870)

name: Papal infallibility

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, he possesses ... that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable.

proposition: When the bishop of Rome solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he is protected from error, and such a definition does not depend on the later consent of the Church.
elements: The Roman see or its bishop cannot err in faith when teaching the whole Church
This protection applies to solemn definitions, not to every statement
Such definitions are binding without needing confirmation by a council or by the churches
precursors: The Roman church has kept the apostolic faith without falling into doctrinal error
Rome's judgment cited as settling a doctrinal dispute
The Church as a whole cannot fail or be overcome by error
Peter's faith will not fail (Luke 22:32) applied to Rome
incompatible: A bishop of Rome taught error in faith and was rightly condemned for it
Rome's doctrinal decisions are binding only when received by a council or by the other churches
No single bishop, including Rome's, can settle a question of faith for the whole Church
queries: the Roman church has never erred
Rome has spoken the case is closed
the faith of Peter will not fail
the apostolic see kept the faith unstained
decision of the bishop of Rome on doctrine
a council judging the bishop of Rome
confirmation of a council by Rome
first_defined: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (18 July 1870)

name: Immaculate Conception of Mary

defined.quote: the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin

proposition: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception, by a unique grace given in view of Christ's merits.
elements: Mary was without original sin, not only without personal sin
This freedom from original sin began at her conception, not at a later cleansing
It was a grace that depended on Christ's redemption
precursors: Mary as wholly holy, pure, or spotless
Mary as the new Eve, contrasted with Eve's disobedience
Mary never committed personal sin
Mary as the pure dwelling or temple prepared for the Word
incompatible: Mary was conceived in original sin like all other people
Mary was cleansed of sin only at the Annunciation or at some later time
Mary committed personal sins or faults, such as doubt or vanity
Christ alone of all human beings was conceived without sin
queries: the virgin free from every stain
Christ alone was born without sin
Mary cleansed by the Holy Spirit
the pure temple of the Word
first_defined: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854)
notes: No council of another tradition has formally condemned this doctrine (most of their confessions predate 1854), so rejected_by is empty; Orthodox and Protestant writers widely reject it.

name: Assumption of Mary

defined.quote: that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.

proposition: At the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.
elements: Mary's earthly life came to an end (by death or otherwise)
Her body did not remain on earth or decay
She was taken, body and soul, into heaven
precursors: Mary's death or 'falling asleep' (Dormition) told as a special event
Mary's body was kept from decay because it bore Christ
Mary's tomb found empty
Mary's exalted place in heaven
incompatible: Mary's body lies buried and awaits the general resurrection like others
No one knows how Mary's life ended and nothing should be claimed
Mary's relics or body are venerated at a known grave
queries: falling asleep of the Mother of God
Mary's body taken up into heaven
Mary's body did not see corruption
first_defined: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1 November 1950)
notes: The Orthodox celebrate the Dormition and generally hold that Mary was taken bodily to heaven, but have not defined it as dogma; Protestant confessions do not address it formally.

name: Purgatory

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Purgatory (1563)
defined.quote: there is a Purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but principally by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar

All who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation; but after death they undergo purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven.

proposition: Some who die in God's grace are not yet fully purified and undergo a purification after death, during which the prayers and offerings of the living help them.
elements: Some of the saved need purification after death before entering heaven
This purification involves a temporary punishment or cleansing (often described as fire)
Prayers, alms and the Eucharist offered by the living help the dead
This state is distinct from, and temporary unlike, the punishment of the damned
precursors: Prayer for the dead, and offering the Eucharist for them
A cleansing fire after death (e.g. readings of 1 Corinthians 3:15)
Sins forgiven in the age to come (Matthew 12:32)
An intermediate state of souls before the final judgment
incompatible: At death every soul goes directly to final rest or final punishment with no cleansing between
Prayers for the dead cannot help them
Nothing remains to be purged in anyone who dies in faith
queries: offering for those who have fallen asleep
saved yet so as through fire
sins forgiven in the world to come
the Eucharist offered for the departed
commemoration of the dead at the altar
first_defined: Council of Lyon II (1274) and Council of Florence (1439); Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563)
notes: The Orthodox pray for the dead and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Decree 18) speaks of release from Hades through prayers and the Eucharist, but Orthodox theologians reject the Latin account of purgatorial satisfaction; Orthodoxy is left out of rejected_by because no Orthodox council condemns it by name.

name: Transubstantiation

defined.quote: that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation
He be, in many other places, sacramentally present to us in his own substance, by a manner of existing, which, though we can scarcely express it in words

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1376 (quoting Trent)
defined.quote: by the consecration of the bread and wine there takes place a change of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord

proposition: At the consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the appearances (species), meaning everything the senses or any physical test can detect, remain unchanged; so the change is not a physical or chemical one.
elements: The underlying substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood
No substance of bread or wine remains after the consecration
The appearances (species) of bread and wine remain: everything the senses can test is unchanged
Christ is present 'substantially', not locally or physically as a body occupies space
precursors: The bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (realist change language)
The Eucharist is the flesh and blood of Christ
The bread and wine are changed, transformed or 'made' the body and blood by the word or the Spirit
What looks and tastes like bread is not bread to faith
A change of the nature of the elements, contrasted with how they appear
incompatible: The bread remains bread after consecration, with Christ present alongside or in it
The bread and wine are only figures, signs or symbols of the body and blood
Christ's body is in heaven and is received only spiritually by faith
The bread and wine are changed in their physical appearance or matter
queries: the bread becomes the body of Christ
it is not bread though it seems bread
symbol of the body and blood
consecration of the bread and wine
flesh of Christ in the Eucharist
grading_rules: Realist language ('becomes', 'is changed into', 'is the body') without the substance/appearance distinction is at most precursor here.
first_defined: Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used the term; Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551) defined it
notes: The shared belief that the gifts truly become Christ's body and blood is graded under 'eucharistic-change'; this entry tests only the Latin explanation by substance and appearances. The Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Decree 17) used 'transubstantiated', and Philaret's Longer Catechism (q. 340) keeps the word while denying that it defines the manner of the change; so Orthodoxy is in neither list.

name: Real change of the bread and wine

defined.source: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, q. 340 (1830s)
defined.quote: the word transubstantiation is not to be taken to define the manner in which the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord; for this none can understand but God

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Epiclesis
defined.quote: And make this bread the precious Body of Your Christ. ... And that which is in this cup the precious Blood of Your Christ. ... Changing them by Your Holy Spirit.
It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament.

proposition: At the consecration the bread and wine truly become, by God's action, the body and blood of Christ, so that they are no longer simply bread and wine, without any claim about how the change happens.
elements: The bread and wine are changed (become, are made) into Christ's body and blood
The change is real, not only a change in meaning or use
God (by the Spirit or by Christ's word) brings about the change at the consecration
After the change the gifts are no longer simply bread and wine
precursors: The Eucharist is called the flesh and blood of Christ
The gifts are 'no longer common bread' after the prayer of thanksgiving
Calling down the Spirit or the Word on the offered gifts
incompatible: The bread and wine remain unchanged in their nature, with Christ's body present together with them
The bread and wine are only figures, signs or symbols of the body and blood
Christ's body is in heaven and is received only spiritually by faith
The change is only in the use or meaning of the bread, not in what it is
queries: the bread becomes the body of Christ
changed into the body and blood
send down your Spirit upon these gifts
the Word makes the bread his body
symbol of the body and blood
the nature of the bread is changed
grading_rules: Realist language ('becomes', 'is changed into', 'is made') counts as explicit here; no account of the manner is required.
'This is my body' or 'the body of Christ' with no word of change or becoming is at most partial.
first_defined: Not defined as a separate dogma; the change is prayed for in the eastern epiclesis and stated by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), the Council of Trent (1551) and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
notes: Kept apart from 'transubstantiation' so the belief Catholics and Orthodox share is not tied to the Latin explanation. Lutherans are in rejected_by because the Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration VII.35) speaks of 'the unchanged essence of the bread', though they affirm the true body is present (see 'sacramental-union'). Anglican Article XXVIII rejects 'the change of the substance of Bread and Wine'.

name: Sacramental union (Lutheran real presence)

defined.quote: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord
We believe, teach, and confess that in the Holy Supper the body and blood of Christ are truly and essentially present, and are truly distributed and received with the bread and wine.

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VII.35 (1577)
defined.quote: under the bread, with the bread, in the bread [the body of Christ is present and offered], are employed, is that by means of them the papistical transubstantiation may be rejected and the sacramental union of the unchanged essence of the bread and of the body of Christ indicated

proposition: In the Lord's Supper Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.
elements: Christ's true body and blood are present in the Supper, not only symbolized or received by faith
The bread and wine remain bread and wine in their essence (no change of substance)
Body and bread are joined in a sacramental union, so that the bread can be called the body
The body is received orally, even by unworthy communicants
precursors: The Eucharist is called the flesh and blood of Christ
The Eucharist consists of two realities, an earthly and a heavenly
The bread keeps its nature after consecration, compared to Christ's human nature kept in the Incarnation
Unworthy communicants also receive the body, to their judgment
incompatible: The bread and wine are changed so that no bread or wine remains
The bread and wine are only figures, signs or symbols of the body and blood
Christ's body is in heaven and is received only spiritually by faith; the unworthy receive only bread
queries: bread and body like the two natures of Christ
the body of Christ received with the bread
the unworthy eat the body to judgment
the bread becomes the body of Christ
grading_rules: A passage counts as explicit only if it holds both that the true body is present and that the bread remains bread.
Realist language alone ('is the body', 'becomes the body') is at most precursor here.
first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530); Formula of Concord, Article VII (1577)
notes: Lutherans reject the label 'consubstantiation', which outsiders often use for this view, so the entry uses their own term. The Orthodox are left out of rejected_by because no Orthodox council condemns it by name, though the Synod of Jerusalem (Decree 17) rejects Lutheran 'impanation'. Anglican Article XXVIII is left out because Anglican views vary.

name: Indulgences

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Indulgences (1563)
defined.quote: the power of conferring Indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church; and she has, even in the most ancient times, used the said power
An indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven

proposition: The Church has authority to grant remission of temporal punishment still owed for sins already forgiven, drawing on the merits of Christ and the saints.
elements: After guilt is forgiven, some temporal punishment for sin may remain
The Church can remit that punishment by its authority
The remission draws on a treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints
Such remission can be applied to the living and (by way of prayer) to the dead
precursors: Penances imposed for sin could be shortened or relaxed by the bishop
Martyrs and confessors interceding for lapsed Christians to be restored early
Satisfaction for sins after baptism through fasting, alms and penance
The merits or prayers of the saints helping other believers
incompatible: Once God forgives sin no punishment of any kind remains
No person or church can lessen the penalty God assigns
The merits of the saints cannot benefit anyone else
queries: relaxing the penance of the lapsed
letters of peace from the martyrs
merits of the martyrs for sinners
first_defined: Clement VI, Unigenitus (1343); Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563)

name: Veneration of icons

defined.quote: Certainly this is not the full adoration {latria} in accordance with our faith, which is properly paid only to the divine nature
the honour paid to an image traverses it, reaching the model, and he who venerates the image, venerates the person represented in that image.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 4 (1672)
defined.quote: the honor paid to the Icon is not at all divided or at all different from [the honor paid to the one who] is portrayed

proposition: Images of Christ, Mary, angels and saints should be set up and given honor (such as a kiss, bowing, incense or lights), an honor that passes to the person depicted and is distinct from the worship due to God alone.
elements: Images of Christ and the saints may rightly be made and displayed in churches
These images should be honored with outward signs (kissing, bowing, lights, incense)
The honor given to an image passes to the person it depicts
This honor differs from the worship (latria) given to God alone
precursors: The Incarnation makes the invisible God visible
Honor given to an image of the emperor passes to the emperor
Pictures or symbols painted in churches or catacombs for teaching
Veneration of the cross, relics or the Gospel book
incompatible: It is wrong to paint images of Christ or the saints
Images must not be set up in churches
Bowing to or honoring any image is idolatry
queries: honor to the image passes to the original
first_defined: Second Council of Nicaea (787); reaffirmed at the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' (843)
notes: Catholics also accept Nicaea II. Lutheran confessions keep images but do not require their veneration, so Lutherans are in neither list. Article XXII of the Thirty-Nine Articles rejects the 'Romish' worship of images.

name: Procession of the Spirit from the Father (against the Filioque)

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 1 (1672)
defined.quote: the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.
The new doctrine, that "the Holy Ghost proceedeth from the Father and the Son," is contrary to the memorable declaration of our LORD
This novel opinion destroys the oneness from the One cause, and the diverse origin of the Persons of the Blessed Trinity

proposition: The Holy Spirit takes his eternal origin from the Father alone as the single source and cause in the Trinity, and does not proceed eternally from the Son as well.
elements: The Father is the one source or cause of both Son and Spirit
The Spirit's eternal procession is from the Father
The Son is not a co-source of the Spirit's eternal being
Nothing should be added to the Creed's 'who proceeds from the Father'
precursors: The Father as the one source (monarchy) of the Godhead
John 15:26 quoted as 'who proceeds from the Father' without mention of the Son
The Spirit is sent into the world by the Son (temporal mission) as distinct from eternal origin
incompatible: The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son
The Spirit has his being from the Son as well as from the Father
Father and Son are together one principle of the Spirit
queries: the Spirit proceeds from the Father
the Father the one source of the Godhead
the Spirit is from the Father and the Son
the Spirit proceeds through the Son
the Spirit receives from the Son
the Spirit is sent by the Son
first_defined: No single conciliar definition; stated against the Latin addition by Photius (9th c.) and formally in the Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848)
notes: Hard case: early 'from the Father through the Son' language is claimed by both sides, so graders should mark it 'precursor' for neither or both, never 'explicit' or 'against'. Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions also hold the Filioque, but only Rome has formally defined it against the East.
grading_rules: The phrase 'from the Father through the Son' is at most precursor here, never explicit and never against.

name: Filioque (procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son)

defined.quote: the holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsistent being from the Father together with the Son, and proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration.
the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son.
The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory, with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God.

proposition: The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from both the Father and the Son, as from one principle.
elements: The Spirit's eternal procession (not only his sending into the world) is from the Son as well as the Father
Father and Son act as one principle in the Spirit's procession
The Son has this from the Father
precursors: The Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son
The Spirit is called 'the Spirit of the Son' or 'of Christ'
The Spirit receives from the Son (John 16:14)
The Spirit is the bond of love between Father and Son
incompatible: The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone
The Father is the only cause of the Spirit's being
The Son has no part in the eternal origin of the Spirit
queries: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son
the Spirit receives from the Son
bond of love between Father and Son
the Father alone is cause of the Spirit
first_defined: Third Council of Toledo (589, local); Council of Lyon II (1274) and Council of Florence (1439) for the Catholic Church
grading_rules: The phrase 'from the Father through the Son' is at most precursor here, never explicit and never against.

name: Distinction between God's essence and energies

defined.source: Metropolitan Hierotheos of Nafpaktos, on the Council of Constantinople of 1351 (2021)
defined.quote: The essence of God is uncreated and the energy of God is uncreated. The Three Persons of the Holy Trinity have the same divine essence, while we participate in the energy of God.

proposition: God's essence is wholly beyond participation, while God's uncreated energies (operations) are truly God and are what creatures share in, without dividing God's simplicity.
elements: God's essence cannot be known or shared by any creature
God's energies or operations are uncreated, not created effects
Creatures truly share in God through the energies (deification)
Distinguishing essence and energies does not divide God
precursors: We know God from his works or operations, not from his essence
God's essence is unknowable and unnamable
The saints become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4)
The light seen at the Transfiguration as divine glory
incompatible: The blessed in heaven see God's very essence
Whatever is in God is simply God's essence with no real distinction
Grace given to creatures is a created gift only
queries: we know God from his operations
the essence of God is unknowable
no one has seen God's essence
God is known by his works not his nature
first_defined: Councils of Constantinople (1341, 1347, 1351), whose decisions were added to the Synodikon of Orthodoxy
notes: No official English text of the 1351 Tome or the Synodikon anathemas could be fetched; the quote is an Orthodox bishop's summary, not the council's words. Catholics have not formally condemned the distinction, so rejected_by is empty.

name: Perpetual virginity of Mary

defined.quote: The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary's real and perpetual virginity even in the act of giving birth to the Son of God made man.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 7 (1672)
defined.quote: being conceived of the Holy Spirit, in the womb of the ever-virgin Mary

proposition: Mary remained a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus for her whole life, and had no other children.
elements: Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin
Her virginity was kept in giving birth
She remained a virgin after Jesus' birth and bore no other children
The 'brothers of the Lord' were not Mary's sons
precursors: The virginal conception of Jesus
Mary called 'the Virgin' as a standing title
The 'brothers of the Lord' explained as Joseph's children or as cousins
Mary as a model for consecrated virgins
incompatible: After Jesus' birth Mary and Joseph had children together
The brothers of the Lord were Mary's own sons
Mary lived as a married woman with Joseph after Jesus' birth
queries: Mary remained a virgin after giving birth
the virgin conceived and the virgin bore
Joseph's sons from a former wife
first_defined: 'Ever-virgin' used at the Second Council of Constantinople (553); Lateran Synod (649)
notes: Luther and early Reformers held this belief and no major Protestant confession formally rejects it, so rejected_by is empty; many modern Protestants reject it in practice.

name: Mary as Mother of God (Theotokos)

defined.source: Council of Ephesus, Cyril's First Anathema (431)
defined.quote: If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore that the holy virgin is the mother of God

defined.source: Council of Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (451)
defined.quote: in the last days the same for us and for our salvation from Mary, the virgin God-bearer as regards his humanity
Hence the Church confesses that Mary is truly "Mother of God" (Theotokos).

proposition: Because the one born of Mary is God the Word made flesh, Mary is rightly called Mother of God (Theotokos), not only mother of Christ's humanity.
elements: The child born of Mary is one person, God the Word
Therefore Mary may be called Mother of God or God-bearer
The title is about Christ's identity, not about Mary being the source of his divinity
precursors: God was born of Mary / God was carried in Mary's womb
Mary as mother of the Lord (Luke 1:43)
Christ is one person, God and man, from Mary
incompatible: Mary should be called mother of Christ, not Mother of God
Mary bore only the man in whom God dwelt
God cannot be said to have been born
queries: God was born of a virgin
God carried in the womb of Mary
mother of Christ not of God
the Word born of the virgin
Mary bore God in the flesh
first_defined: Council of Ephesus (431); confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon (451)
notes: The title stands in the Chalcedonian Definition, which Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions also receive; it is distinctive of Catholics and Orthodox mainly in devotional use. No tradition formally rejects it.

name: Invocation of the saints

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, On the invocation of saints (1563)
defined.quote: the saints, who reign together with Christ, offer up their own prayers to God for men; that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them, and to have recourse to their prayers, aid, (and) help

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 8 (1672)
defined.quote: Notwithstanding, in [our] prayers and supplications unto Him, we say the Saints are intercessors, and, above all, the undefiled Mother of the very God the Word

proposition: The saints in heaven pray for the living, and it is right for Christians to address the saints directly and ask for their prayers.
elements: The departed saints are aware of and pray for those on earth
Christians may directly address departed saints
Asking saints for their prayers does not detract from Christ as the one mediator
precursors: The martyrs and departed saints pray for the Church
Remembering the saints at the Eucharist
Gathering at martyrs' tombs for their feast days
Asking living Christians to pray for one another
incompatible: Prayer must be addressed to God alone, never to a departed saint
The dead know nothing of what happens on earth
Calling on the saints takes honor from Christ the one mediator
queries: remember us in your prayers blessed one
the saints pray for the living
do the dead know what happens here
prayer at the tomb of the martyr
first_defined: Second Council of Nicaea (787) assumes it; Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

name: The Eucharist as a sacrifice

defined.quote: If any one saith, that in the mass a true and proper sacriflce is not offered to God; or, that to be offered is nothing else but that Christ is given us to eat; let him be anathema.
The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 17 (1672)
defined.quote: it is a true and propitiatory Sacrifice offered for all Orthodox, living and dead

proposition: In the Eucharist the Church offers to God a true sacrifice, one with Christ's sacrifice on the cross, which benefits the living and the dead.
elements: The Eucharist is a sacrifice offered to God, not only a meal received
It is the same sacrifice as the cross, offered without bloodshed
It is offered by priests for the living and the dead and obtains mercy (propitiatory)
precursors: The Eucharist as the 'pure offering' of Malachi 1:11
The Eucharist called an offering, oblation or sacrifice of praise
The bishop or presbyter as one who 'offers the gifts'
The altar language used of the Lord's table
incompatible: In the Supper nothing is offered to God except praise and thanksgiving
Christ's sacrifice was once for all and is not offered again in any form
The Supper is only a remembrance of a past sacrifice
queries: the priest offers the body of Christ
the one sacrifice once for all
first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 22 (1562); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
notes: Hard case: many early writers use 'sacrifice' and 'offering' for the Eucharist, and Protestants accept a 'sacrifice of praise'; graders should count only a sacrifice offered to God for sins or for the dead as 'explicit'.
grading_rules: Calling the Eucharist an offering, sacrifice or thanksgiving is precursor; explicit needs a sacrifice offered to God for sins, or for the living and the dead.

name: Seven sacraments

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 7, Canon 1 on the Sacraments (1547)
defined.quote: If any one saith, that the sacraments of the New Law were not all instituted by Jesus Christ, our Lord; or, that they are more, or less, than seven, to wit, Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 15 (1672)
defined.quote: We believe that there are in the Church Evangelical Mysteries [ i.e., Sacraments of the Gospel Dispensation], and that they are seven.

proposition: Christ instituted exactly seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation (chrismation), Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders and marriage.
elements: There is a defined class of sacraments (mysteries) instituted by Christ
Confirmation, penance, anointing, orders and marriage are sacraments alongside baptism and the Eucharist
The number is exactly seven
precursors: Anointing with chrism after baptism
Laying on of hands to ordain clergy
Anointing of the sick by presbyters (James 5:14)
Public penance and reconciliation by the bishop
Marriage called a mystery (Ephesians 5:32)
incompatible: Christ instituted only two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper
Marriage, orders or anointing are good rites but not sacraments
queries: laying on of hands for the Spirit
anointing of the sick with oil
first_defined: Council of Lyon II (1274); Council of Florence (1439); Council of Trent, Session 7 (1547)
notes: No early writer lists exactly seven; the list dates from the 12th century (Peter Lombard). Expect mostly 'precursor' results, which is the honest outcome.
grading_rules: Naming or honouring individual rites is precursor; explicit needs a fixed list of seven sacraments.

name: Scripture alone as final authority (sola scriptura)

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm, 1 (1577)
defined.quote: the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone

The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation: so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith

proposition: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith; councils, fathers and traditions are to be judged by it, and nothing not taught in or provable from Scripture may be required as necessary belief.
elements: Scripture contains all that is necessary for salvation
Nothing may be required as an article of faith unless it can be proved from Scripture
Scripture is the final judge over councils, fathers and church traditions
Unwritten apostolic traditions are not a second, equal source of doctrine
precursors: Scripture is sufficient for teaching the faith
Doctrine must be proved from the Scriptures
Even a bishop's or council's teaching is to be tested by Scripture
Heretics are refuted from Scripture
incompatible: Some necessary doctrines are known only from unwritten apostolic tradition
Scripture and tradition are to be received with equal reverence
The Church's tradition or a council judges the meaning of Scripture with final authority
queries: do not believe me unless I prove it from scripture
we have the scriptures what need of more
councils must be judged by scripture
first_defined: Formula of Concord (1577); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)
notes: Hard case: early writers often call Scripture sufficient and also appeal to unwritten tradition and the 'rule of faith'. Graders must not treat praise of Scripture alone as 'explicit'; the doctrine's distinctive claim is that Scripture is the only final norm.
grading_rules: Praise of Scripture as true, holy or sufficient is not explicit by itself; explicit needs Scripture set as the only binding rule. An appeal to unwritten tradition as binding counts as against.

name: Justification by faith alone (sola fide)

defined.quote: men cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works, but are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith

We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ by Faith, and not for our own works or deservings: Wherefore, that we are justified by Faith only is a most wholesome Doctrine

proposition: A person is justified (declared righteous) before God through faith alone, apart from any works, though such faith then produces good works.
elements: Justification is received through faith, not earned by works
Faith is the only means by which justification is received (no works joined to it as a cause)
Good works follow justification as its fruit, not as its ground
precursors: We are saved by faith, not by works (Paul's language repeated)
Justified by faith alone, used of the thief on the cross or of Abraham
Salvation is a free gift of grace
Works of the Law do not justify
incompatible: We are justified by faith and works together
Faith without love does not justify
Justification increases through good works
queries: saved by faith not by works
the thief on the cross was saved by faith
Abraham believed and it was counted as righteousness
first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article IV (1530); Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XI (1563/1571)
notes: Hard case: some early writers use the words 'faith alone' (sola fide) in contexts that may mean faith without the ritual Law, not the Reformation sense. Graders should check the meaning, not only the phrase. Trent (Session 6, Canon 9) and the Synod of Jerusalem (Decree 13) formally reject it.
grading_rules: Judge the meaning, not the words: 'faith alone' used against works of the Mosaic law, or meaning faith as the start of salvation, is at most partial.

name: Imputed righteousness

defined.quote: that God forgives us our sins out of pure grace, without any work, merit, or worthiness of ours preceding, present, or following, that He presents and imputes to us the righteousness of Christ's obedience
not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous

proposition: In justification God counts Christ's own righteousness as belonging to the believer, so that the believer is declared righteous on that basis, not because of a righteousness worked within him.
elements: Justification is a declaration (legal verdict), not a process of inner renewal
The ground of the verdict is Christ's righteousness credited to the believer
Inner renewal (sanctification) follows but is not the basis of being justified
precursors: A 'sweet exchange': Christ takes our sin and we receive his righteousness
Faith reckoned as righteousness (Romans 4)
Sins not counted against the sinner
Justify used in a legal sense, to declare righteous
incompatible: To be justified is to be made righteous inwardly by grace poured into the heart
Our righteousness before God is the love the Spirit works in us
queries: made righteous by the Spirit within
clothed in the righteousness of Christ
first_defined: Formula of Concord (1577); Westminster Confession, 11.1 (1646)
notes: Trent (Session 6, Canon 11) rejects justification 'by the sole imputation of the justice of Christ'.

name: Double predestination

defined.quote: By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life; and others foreordained to everlasting death.

The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy, as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by

defined.source: Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 15 (1619)
defined.quote: not all people have been chosen but that some have not been chosen or have been passed by in God's eternal election

proposition: Before creation God, by his free decree and not because of foreseen faith or works, chose some people for eternal life and passed by the rest, leaving them to just condemnation for their sins.
elements: God's choice of the elect is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith or merit
God also decreed to pass by the non-elect
The non-elect are condemned for their own sins
The number of the elect is fixed
precursors: Election by grace, not by works
God gives perseverance only to some, for reasons hidden in his will
A fixed number of the predestined
The 'mass of perdition' from which God freely saves some
incompatible: God predestines people because he foresees their faith or merits
God wills all people to be saved and gives all sufficient grace
No one is passed over by God; each decides his own end
queries: God wills all to be saved
election not by works but by grace
Jacob I loved Esau I hated
first_defined: Synod of Dort (1619); Westminster Confession (1646)
notes: The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, ch. 3) holds a similar view, so Particular (Reformed) Baptists share it. Formula of Concord, Epitome XI.4 limits predestination to 'the godly, beloved children of God'.

name: Spiritual real presence in the Lord's Supper

defined.quote: the body and blood of Christ being then, not corporally or carnally, in, with, or under the bread and wine; yet, as really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers in that ordinance
The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the Body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is Faith.
spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death

proposition: In the Lord's Supper believers truly receive Christ's body and blood, but spiritually, by faith, not because Christ's body is physically in or under the bread.
elements: Believers truly receive Christ and his benefits in the Supper
Christ's body is not physically in, with, or under the bread
The means of receiving is faith, by the Spirit
Unbelievers receive only the outward signs
precursors: Eating Christ's flesh means believing in him (John 6 read spiritually)
Lift up your hearts: Christ is received above, in heaven
The bread called a figure or sign of the body while still giving grace
The wicked do not truly eat Christ's body
incompatible: The bread itself becomes or contains Christ's body, which even unbelievers receive
The Supper is only a reminder and no one receives Christ in it
queries: eat the flesh of Christ by faith
the wicked do not eat the body of Christ
the body of Christ is in heaven
first_defined: Consensus Tigurinus (1549); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)
notes: Kept separate from the memorial view because the Reformed and Anglican texts say believers truly receive Christ, which the memorial view does not claim. The 1689 Baptist Confession also holds this view.

name: The Lord's Supper as a memorial

defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church, through partaking of the bread and the fruit of the vine, memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming.

proposition: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act in which believers remember Christ's death; the bread and wine represent his body and blood and are not a means by which his body is present or received.
elements: The Supper's main purpose is remembrance of Christ's death
The bread and wine are symbols or signs of the body and blood
No presence of Christ's body is tied to the elements
precursors: Do this in remembrance of me, stressed as the Supper's purpose
The bread called a figure or symbol of the body
The Supper as a thanksgiving and a pledge of unity
incompatible: The bread becomes or truly is Christ's body
In the Supper believers truly receive Christ's body and blood
The Supper is a sacrifice offered to God
queries: symbol of the body and blood
first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523); Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 2000)
notes: Zwinglian and modern Baptist memorialism merged into one entry because their texts make the same claim. Not all Baptists hold it: the 1689 Confession teaches spiritual presence. The Reformed and Anglican confessions also reject a 'bare memorial', but are left out of rejected_by because they do not condemn it by name.

name: Believer's baptism only

defined.quote: Those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: Christian baptism is the immersion of a believer in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

proposition: Only those who personally profess repentance and faith should be baptized, so infants are not proper subjects of baptism.
elements: Baptism should follow a personal profession of faith
Infants, who cannot profess faith, should not be baptized
Immersion is the proper mode (held by most who hold this view)
precursors: Instruction and fasting before baptism (catechumenate)
Baptism described as a pledge or confession made by the candidate
Delaying baptism, including of children, until they can understand
Baptism by going down into the water
incompatible: Infants should be baptized
Little children are to be brought to baptism, with others answering for them
Baptism of infants comes from the apostles
queries: let them come when they can know Christ
the catechumens are taught before baptism
those who answer for the children
baptism of infants from the apostles
first_defined: Schleitheim Confession (1527, Anabaptist); First London Baptist Confession (1644); Second London Confession (1689)

name: Gathered, self-governing congregation

defined.quote: To each of these churches thus gathered, according to his mind declared in his word, he hath given all that power and authority, which is in any way needful for their carrying on that order in worship and discipline

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VI (2000)
defined.quote: A New Testament church of the Lord Jesus Christ is an autonomous local congregation of baptized believers, associated by covenant in the faith and fellowship of the gospel

proposition: Each local congregation of professing believers holds full authority from Christ to govern itself, choose its own officers and exercise discipline, without a higher church authority over it.
elements: The church is made up of professing believers who have joined by consent (gathered)
Each local congregation holds full authority from Christ
The congregation chooses its own officers by common vote
No bishop or synod has authority over the local church
precursors: The whole congregation chooses or approves its clergy
The church as a gathered community of saints, separate from the world
Discipline exercised by the gathered church (Matthew 18)
Local churches as each complete, with their own presbyters
incompatible: The bishop alone holds authority over the local church
Nothing may be done in the church without the bishop
A synod or council of bishops can rule over local churches
queries: chosen by the vote of the people
first_defined: Cambridge Platform (1648, Congregationalist); Second London Baptist Confession, ch. 26 (1689)
notes: Hard case: early 'election by the people' fits several church orders, so it is only a precursor. Reformed and Anglican churches also differ from it (presbyterian and episcopal government) but do not condemn it by name.
grading_rules: Election of clergy by the people, or the people's consent, is precursor only; explicit needs each local congregation to govern itself without authority above it.

name: Infant baptism

defined.quote: Born with a fallen human nature and tainted by original sin, children also have need of the new birth in Baptism
children are to be baptized who, being offered to God through Baptism are received into God's grace.
Not only those that do actually profess faith in and obedience unto Christ, but also the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized.

proposition: Infants of Christian parents should be baptized, and are properly received into the Church by baptism before they can profess faith themselves.
elements: Infants may and should be baptized
Their baptism is valid without their own profession of faith
Baptism benefits infants (by forgiveness, grace or covenant membership)
precursors: Whole households baptized
Baptism as the new circumcision
Children brought to Christ and blessed
Infants share in original sin and need cleansing
incompatible: Baptism should be delayed until a person can believe
Infants have no need of baptism
Only those who confess faith may be baptized
queries: baptism of children from the apostles
do not delay the baptism of infants
first_defined: Council of Carthage (418) condemned denial of infant baptism for forgiveness; Augsburg Confession (1530); Council of Trent (1547); Westminster Confession (1646)

name: Apostolic succession of bishops

defined.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors. They gave them their own position of teaching authority.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 10 (1672)
defined.quote: he, as a successor of the Apostles, having received in continued succession by the imposition of hands and the invocation of the All-holy Spirit the grace that is given him of the Lord of binding and loosing

defined.source: Book of Common Prayer, Preface to the Ordinal (1662)
defined.quote: It is evident unto all men diligently reading holy Scripture and ancient Authors, that from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church; Bishops, Priests, and Deacons.

proposition: Bishops are successors of the apostles through an unbroken line of ordination by laying on of hands, and this succession is needed for a church's ministry to be fully valid.
elements: The apostles appointed bishops as their successors
The succession passes by ordination with laying on of hands, in an unbroken line
The threefold ministry of bishops, presbyters and deacons comes from the apostles
Succession guards the apostolic teaching and the validity of the sacraments
precursors: Lists of bishops going back to the apostles
Appeal to churches founded by apostles as guardians of true teaching
Bishops, presbyters and deacons as distinct offices
Ordination by the laying on of hands
incompatible: Bishops and presbyters are the same office
A congregation can ordain its own ministers without a bishop
True succession is of doctrine only, not of persons
queries: succession of bishops from the apostles
list of the bishops of Rome
bishop and presbyter are the same
first_defined: Not a single defined dogma; affirmed by the Council of Trent, Session 23 (1563), the Anglican Ordinal (1550/1662), and the Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 10 (1672)
notes: Lutheran churches vary (Scandinavian Lutherans kept episcopal succession; others did not) and their confessions do not require it, so Lutherans are in neither list.

name: A closed canon of Scripture

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 4, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
defined.quote: receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament
All which are given by inspiration of God to be the rule of faith and life.
In the name of the holy Scripture we do understand those Canonical Books of the Old and New Testament, of whose authority was never any doubt in the Church.

proposition: The Church holds a fixed list of inspired books as Scripture, including the 27 books of the New Testament, distinct from all other Christian writings.
elements: There is a defined list of books recognized as Scripture
The New Testament comprises the four Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation (27 books)
Other Christian writings, however respected, are not Scripture
precursors: Four Gospels and only four
Lists of 'acknowledged' and 'disputed' books
Books read publicly in church versus books for private reading
Rejection of particular gospels or writings as spurious
incompatible: Writings such as the Shepherd of Hermas or 1 Clement are Scripture
A New Testament book such as Revelation, Hebrews or 2 Peter is not Scripture
queries: the four gospels and no more
the books of the New Testament
the Shepherd is not among the scriptures
first_defined: Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 (367) gives the 27-book New Testament; local councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397); Trent (1546), Article VI (1563), Westminster (1646)
notes: Canons differ: all major traditions share the 27-book New Testament, but the Old Testament differs (see 'deuterocanonical-books'). Ethiopian and other Oriental churches use wider canons. Graders should grade New Testament statements here and Old Testament ones there.

name: Deuterocanonical books as Scripture

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 4, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
defined.quote: Tobias, Judith, Esther, Job, the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms; the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Canticle of Canticles, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 3 (1672)
defined.quote: For we judge these also to be with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture genuine parts of Scripture.
The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture

proposition: Books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1-2 Maccabees belong to the Old Testament as inspired Scripture, on the same footing as the other books.
elements: These books are inspired Scripture
They may be used to establish doctrine
They stand on the same level as the books of the Hebrew canon
precursors: Quoting Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit or Maccabees with 'Scripture says'
These books read publicly in church
These books included in early lists or codices of Scripture
incompatible: The Old Testament is limited to the books of the Hebrew canon
These books are useful for reading but not for proving doctrine
Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit or Judith are not in the canon
queries: as it is written in Wisdom
books outside the canon read to catechumens
the twenty-two books of the Hebrews
first_defined: Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), local; Council of Florence (1442); Council of Trent (1546); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
notes: Anglican Article VI and Lutheran practice keep these books for reading 'for example of life' but 'not to establish any doctrine', a middle position; so Anglicans and Lutherans are in neither list. Writers such as Jerome reject them as canon while others such as Augustine accept them, so expect mixed results.
